lessons.title: The WordPress Content Model
lessons.content:
# The WordPress Content Model

WordPress organizes content around posts, pages, custom post types, taxonomies, users, and media.

### Core ideas
- Posts are time-oriented content entries.
- Pages are usually static site sections.
- Custom post types model domain-specific content.
- Taxonomies group content for browsing and filtering.

### Practical takeaway
A clean content model matters early. If products, events, and testimonials all become regular posts, the admin experience gets messy fast.

lessons.title: Themes, Templates, and the Loop
lessons.content:
# Themes, Templates, and the Loop

Themes control how WordPress content is presented.

### Key pieces
- Template files define page structure.
- The Loop iterates over queried posts.
- Template tags output post data, metadata, and navigation.

### Engineering rule
Keep display logic in templates and reusable behavior in functions, hooks, or plugins. Mixing everything into one file becomes hard to maintain.

lessons.title: Plugins and Hooks
lessons.content:
# Plugins and Hooks

WordPress is extensible through plugins plus its action and filter hook systems.

### Hook types
- Actions let you run code at specific points.
- Filters let you modify data before it is used or displayed.

### Practical note
Choose plugins for reusable behavior and keep theme code focused on presentation. That separation helps when themes change later.

lessons.title: Custom Post Types and Taxonomies
lessons.content:
# Custom Post Types and Taxonomies

Custom post types let WordPress handle domain-specific records such as movies, products, courses, or portfolios.

### Related concept
Taxonomies provide structured grouping such as genres, topics, or skill levels.

### Design rule
Pick singular and plural names carefully, because these labels shape the admin interface and affect developer clarity over time.

lessons.title: Custom Fields and Metadata
lessons.content:
# Custom Fields and Metadata

WordPress stores extra structured values as post meta, term meta, user meta, or options.

### Use cases
- Event dates
- Product SKUs
- Hero banners
- Per-page settings

### Caution
Meta fields are flexible but easy to abuse. Define consistent keys and validation rules so data stays predictable.

lessons.title: Menus, Widgets, and Block Editing
lessons.content:
# Menus, Widgets, and Block Editing

Modern WordPress sites often combine classic theme concepts with block-based editing.

### Main areas
- Navigation menus define site structure.
- Widgets or widget areas surface reusable sidebar or footer content.
- Blocks let editors compose richer page layouts.

### Team rule
Protect editors from accidental complexity. A smaller set of purposeful blocks is usually better than exposing every possible layout control.

lessons.title: WordPress Security Basics
lessons.content:
# WordPress Security Basics

WordPress security depends on updates, capability checks, validation, and output escaping.

### Important practices
- Keep core, themes, and plugins updated.
- Validate and sanitize incoming data.
- Escape output in templates.
- Check user capabilities before sensitive actions.

### Practical rule
Most WordPress security issues come from weak custom code or stale plugins, not from the CMS concept itself.

lessons.title: Performance and Caching
lessons.content:
# Performance and Caching

WordPress performance depends on hosting quality, database usage, media size, plugin load, and caching strategy.

### Typical optimizations
- Page caching
- Object caching where available
- Image optimization
- Query reduction
- Avoiding plugin bloat

### Review habit
Profile slow pages before guessing. Sometimes the issue is a single expensive query or plugin hook rather than the whole theme.

lessons.title: The REST API and Headless Use Cases
lessons.content:
# The REST API and Headless Use Cases

WordPress can expose content through its REST API for use in JavaScript frontends or external systems.

### Common reasons to go headless
- Custom frontends
- Mobile apps
- Shared content across platforms
- More control over rendering

### Tradeoff
Headless architecture can improve flexibility, but it also moves preview, caching, SEO, and editorial workflow complexity elsewhere.
